Platform comparison

Duda vs WordPress

The real difference is not features. It is who carries the maintenance burden after launch, and whether your client can safely edit their own site.

By Carl Madelo, Certified Duda Professional 8 min read Updated 2026-08-24

Almost every business I migrate to Duda is coming off WordPress, and almost none of them left because WordPress could not do what they needed. They left because a plugin update broke the contact form, or the person who built the site stopped answering emails, or the theme they bought in 2019 stopped receiving updates. WordPress is the most capable website platform in existence and it is also the one that asks the most of whoever owns it. Duda is the opposite trade: a narrower ceiling, but almost nothing to maintain. Which of those trades is correct depends entirely on whether you have someone whose job it is to look after the site.

Duda vs WordPress at a build level
CriterionDudaAlternative
Ongoing maintenance Platform updates handled by Duda. Nothing to patch on your side. Core, theme and plugin updates are the site owner's responsibility, indefinitely.
Client editing safety Content editing is sandboxed — a client cannot break the layout by editing text. Depends entirely on how the theme or page builder was configured. Often fragile.
Extensibility ceiling Widget Builder and custom code cover most needs, but you work inside Duda's model. Effectively unlimited. Anything you can build in PHP, you can build here.
Complex functionality Memberships, basic ecommerce, forms, scheduling. Heavier logic needs external tools. Mature plugin ecosystem for LMS, marketplaces, complex ecommerce, custom post types.
Performance out of the box Managed CDN and image handling by default. Fast without configuration. Achievable, but requires caching, image optimisation and hosting decisions.
Data portability Export is limited. Moving off Duda means a rebuild. Full database and file access. You own everything.
Multi-site management Built for it — team accounts, reusable templates, one dashboard. Multisite exists but is operationally heavy at agency scale.
Security exposure Managed platform. No plugin supply chain to audit. Every plugin is a dependency you inherit. This is the single biggest real-world risk.

Where WordPress genuinely wins

If your site needs to do something unusual, WordPress will do it and Duda probably will not. Course platforms with drip content, marketplaces with vendor payouts, ecommerce with complex tax and shipping rules, membership tiers with conditional content, anything that needs a custom database table — that is WordPress territory and pretending otherwise wastes everyone's time.

The second real advantage is ownership. A WordPress site is a database and a folder of files that you control. If you fall out with your developer, you take the site elsewhere. Duda is a hosted platform: leaving means rebuilding. For some businesses that lock-in is an acceptable trade for not having to think about the site again. For others it is disqualifying, and that is a reasonable position.

Where Duda wins in practice

The advantage that actually shows up in client relationships is that nothing rots. A Duda site built in 2023 still works in 2026 without anyone touching it. A WordPress site left alone for three years is a liability — outdated plugins, a PHP version the host no longer supports, and a login screen that has been getting probed daily the entire time.

The second is that clients can edit their own content without supervision. Duda separates content from layout properly, so a client updating an opening-hours line cannot accidentally delete a section or push the footer through the middle of the page. That single property removes most of the small, unbillable support requests that make small-business web work unprofitable.

How I decide on a project

I ask one question first: after launch, who is responsible for this site? If the answer is a named person whose job includes it, WordPress is viable and its ceiling is worth having. If the answer is 'the owner, when they remember', Duda is the safer recommendation almost every time.

The second question is whether the site needs to do anything a brochure-plus-CMS cannot do. Service pages, location pages, project galleries, blog, forms, booking links, basic ecommerce — Duda handles all of it comfortably. The moment the brief includes custom application logic, I refer the project on rather than force it.

The verdict

Choose WordPress if you need functionality beyond a marketing site, if you have technical maintenance covered, or if full data ownership is non-negotiable.

Choose Duda if the site's job is to present a business and generate enquiries, if nobody on your side wants to think about updates, and if a non-technical person needs to edit content safely.

For the construction, home-services and property clients I usually work with, Duda is the right answer roughly nine times in ten — not because it is more capable, but because the failure mode of an unmaintained WordPress site is so much worse than the failure mode of hitting Duda's ceiling.

Frequently asked questions

Can I move my WordPress content to Duda?

Yes. Pages, posts, images and metadata all transfer. What does not transfer is plugin-driven functionality, so the first step of any migration is auditing which plugins are actually load-bearing and finding a Duda-native or third-party equivalent for each.

Will I lose my Google rankings switching from WordPress to Duda?

Not if the migration is done properly. Rankings are lost when URLs change without redirects, or when heading structure and metadata are rebuilt from scratch. A migration with a complete 301 map and preserved on-page structure typically sees no lasting change in organic traffic.

Is Duda cheaper than WordPress?

The licence cost is usually higher and the total cost is usually lower, because WordPress's real expense is maintenance, security and the developer time spent on breakages rather than hosting. Compare three-year totals rather than monthly figures.

Can I add custom code to a Duda site?

Yes. Duda supports custom HTML, CSS and JavaScript at site and page level, plus reusable custom widgets through the Widget Builder. It is not as open as a PHP codebase, but it covers considerably more than most people assume.
